label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# The Last Toast

I did my last night shift on Saturday. Twenty-one to half seven, majors, the usual mix of chest pain, falls, and someone who had been waiting since teatime and wanted it known. Nothing dramatic happened. That's how I'd want to remember it, I think, if I get to choose.

Fourteen years of nights. My first one was in 2012, as an SHO, carrying a bleep that went off so often I started to feel it when it didn't. I was twenty-eight and sure I'd be doing this for a few years before "real" life started. Real life turned out to be this: the department between nine at night and eight in the morning, when the building changes its character.

From Monday I'm on days only. My knees have been arguing with the stairs for a while now, my sleep has been, at best, a rumour, and the GP looked at my blood pressure readings and stopped making jokes about it. All of that is true, and all of it is good reason. I'm relieved. I'm also a bit ashamed of how relieved I am, which is its own story.

---

I want to be honest about what nights gave me, because I think it's easy to forget the good parts once you're out.

Nights gave me a particular kind of attention. Fewer managers, fewer emails, fewer people with opinions about the flow board. At three in the morning it was just us, the patients, and whatever we could manage together. Decisions got made fast and nobody pretended otherwise. If I got something wrong I said so, and someone said "right, what next," and we did what next. I have never been more honest at work than I was on nights, and I think the same is true of most of the people I worked with. The department is most itself in those hours. Less polish, more truth, and a lot more kindness, usually without anyone announcing it.

People outside medicine often assume nights run on adrenaline. Some of it does. But mostly, from what I can tell, it's about staying kind at five in the morning when you're completely empty. The skill isn't in the big resuscitation, which you hardly ever get to do alone anyway. It's in the fifth conversation of the shift, when you're tired and the person in front of you is frightened, and you still take the extra minute to sit down.

And nights gave me Folasade.

Folasade has been our charge nurse on nights for twenty-two years. Twenty-two. She knows where everything is, who is going to be trouble before they've arrived, and which consultant needs a phone call and which one needs to be left alone. She is also still faster than me on the stairs, and she will tell you so. I have watched her calm a relative, redirect a registrar, and find a bed that everyone else swore didn't exist, all before the kettle boiled. If I ever learn to do half of that, I'll count it as the best thing nights gave me.

---

Then there's the toast.

At about four in the morning someone always makes toast in the staff room. It's not a rota item or a policy. It's simply what happens. You come in from a bay, and there's a smell of bread and a plate with a few slices going cold on the side, and somebody says "who's had the toast?" Nobody has ever admitted to starting it. I've asked. Everyone shrugs. I'm now fairly sure it's a collective sort of haunting, and I'm going to miss it more than I expected.

I'm also going to miss the cold. The first winter I worked nights, I sat in my car in the Infirmary car park at the end of a shift and cried, because I couldn't remember whether I had given the second dose of something. I went back in and checked. I had. The frost on the windscreen was thick enough that I couldn't see the lamp posts, and I sat there with the engine running until the glass cleared. I think about that car park more than I'd like to admit. I was so frightened of making a mistake that I forgot I was allowed to be a person doing a hard job. It took me years to learn the difference, and nights taught me most of what I know about it.

Last winter, around three in the morning, an older man I had been looking after held my hand. He told me I had his daughter's hands. I don't remember what I said back. He went home a few days later, and I think about him more than I expected to. I'm not going to say more than that, because it's his and not mine to tell. But I wanted to note it here, because it's the sort of moment you only get on nights, and it's part of what I'm taking with me.

---

Driving home on Sunday morning, I came down London Road with the sun coming up over the rooftops. Radio 4 was playing the shipping forecast on catch-up, and I was listening to it the way I always do after a night, letting the names roll past without really hearing them. Dogger, Fisher, German Bight. I'd heard that same broadcast a few hundred times from the same seat. It hit me then that I would not see that particular light from that side of the road again, at least not in the same way. Some part of me is still there, I suspect, at the same junction at seven-thirty on a Sunday, looking for it.

I missed both of my nieces' naming ceremonies because I was on nights. I watched the first one on a video call from the staff room, with a cup of tea going cold beside me, and I could hardly see the screen for the people walking past behind me. My sister never once complained. Not once, through all the missed birthdays and the weekends I couldn't come, and the phone calls at odd hours from different time zones. She just kept asking when I'd be free, and kept meaning it. I owe her more than a blog post can cover, but I'm going to try to do better now that the hours will line up with everyone else's.

---

So that's where I am. Relieved, grateful, a bit sore, and not quite sure what to do with my body at night now that I'm not expected to be awake. I keep reaching for the bleep that isn't there. I keep waking at three and checking the time. I expect that will settle, the way most things do.

What I'll keep is the honesty of those hours, the kindness that needed no audience, the people who taught me more than any course did, and the particular way a department feels when most of the building is asleep and the ones who are awake have decided to look after each other.

And I'll keep the toast. Someone on the next rota will make it at four o'clock, and nobody will admit to it. Good. Let that stay a mystery. Folasade will be on the stairs, probably ahead of everyone, and she will still be the one who knows where everything is.

reasons: It says the doctor watched one niece's naming ceremony on video, whereas the request says both were missed over video.
